messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 77

He is 58, a North American man who has spent most of his adult life as a dentist, a profession that depends on steadiness, precision, and a calm manner with other people’s fear. For years, he is the kind of man who can lean over a chair with his hands steady and his voice even, explaining a procedure while someone grips the armrests. In his own life, however, he has become less steady since the night police violence enters his story and divides it into before and after.

The event happens in a context that still feels, to him, unbearably ordinary. He is out in public when an interaction with police escalates with a speed he cannot fully follow. He recalls the sudden shift in tone, the shouting, the hard certainty in the officers’ movements, and then the physical force that leaves him shocked more than anything else at first. What stays with him is not only pain, but humiliation and disbelief: the sense that his body is being handled as if he does not belong to himself. He remembers the sound of his own voice changing, becoming higher and more frightened than he recognizes, and how quickly that fear turns into a kind of helpless, animal panic. Even now, when he tells the story, he keeps returning to one detail at a time, as if he still cannot find the full shape of what happened.

Afterward, he is physically shaken and mentally scrambled in a way he does not expect. At first he tries to push through. He goes back to work, because he has patients scheduled and an office to run, and because stopping feels too much like surrender. But the body keeps its own record. He startles at sudden noises in the clinic, especially the sharp crack of a dropped metal tray or an unexpected knock at the door. He notices himself scanning for exits whenever he enters a room, even though he has no plan for what he would do if he had to use one. The white coats, the badge-shaped name tags, the sight of uniformed security in public places can make his chest tighten before he is consciously aware of why. He begins to feel that his nerves are living too close to the surface.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to break down. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes in the dark with his heart racing, already bracing for something he cannot name. He has dreams that are not exact repeats of the event but share its helplessness: hands on him, commands he cannot answer fast enough, the certainty that he is being judged and overpowered. In the morning he feels as if he has not rested at all. He drinks more coffee than he used to, partly to function, partly to keep moving so he does not have to sit still with his thoughts.

He becomes more irritable with the people closest to him, then feels ashamed about it. He is in a relationship, and the person he is with notices first that he is less available, more clipped, quicker to withdraw after a difficult day. He can talk for an hour with a patient about restorative options and then come home and answer a simple question with visible frustration. He does not like the way he hears himself. Sometimes he shuts down entirely, sitting in silence and staring at the television without taking anything in. At other times he is flooded with anger that feels out of proportion to the trigger, but when he looks closely, the anger is attached to something older and more helpless: the feeling that he was treated as if his fear and dignity did not matter.

He also notices that he no longer moves through the world with his old confidence. He avoids situations that might place him near police, crowds, or anywhere he could be trapped. He rethinks routes, parks in places that allow a quick exit, and chooses seats with his back to the wall. He tells himself this is just being careful, but privately he knows it is fear organizing his days. At work, he can still function, yet it takes more effort to remain present with patients when his own mind is pulling him back to the event. Some days he catches himself clenching his jaw so tightly that his face aches by midday. He is aware, in a quiet and painful way, that his profession requires him to help other people feel safe while he himself no longer feels safe in his own skin.

Over time, he becomes more reflective, though not less affected. He can describe the event now with more coherence than he could at first, but describing it does not make it feel distant. It remains close enough to shape how he sleeps, how he drives, how he listens for footsteps outside a room. He is still the man who shows up for his patients and tries to be dependable, and he is also the man who carries a deep, unshakable sense that something in him was broken open by what happened and has not yet settled back into place.
